Named after the famous casino, the Monte Carlo method uses pseudo-random numbers to simulate millions of individual, hypothetical particle interactions one-by-one according to the laws of quantum mechanics and classical physics. By aggregating millions of these simulated events, we build up predicted histograms that can be directly compared with real experimental data.

children.value: Once the secondary particles leave the atomic nucleus, they travel through the detector medium. Software toolkits like GEANT4

Charged particles (like muons or electrons) lose kinetic energy as they pass through matter by knocking electrons off surrounding atoms (ionisation) or emitting radiation. GEANT4 steps each particle forward by a small distance

children.html: Δx\Delta xΔx

children.value: and subtracts energy using stopping-power equations (e.g., the Bethe-Bloch formula).

The lost energy is converted into detectable signals based on detector technology—for instance, Cherenkov light cones in water, scintillation photons, or drifted ionisation electrons in high-voltage fields.
GEANT4 tracks particles through precise 3D CAD models of the apparatus, accounting for dead regions, structural support walls, and physical boundaries where particles might escape unmeasured.

The raw, simulated signals (photon hits, wire charges) pass through the exact same reconstruction code used for real experimental data. The algorithms re-cluster light hits and fit tracks to output a final
